<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>moved the adoption of the recommendations.</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to.</p>

<p>The committee&#x2019;s report was set down for consideration to-morrow.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#prisons_and_reformatories_bill_in_committee">

<heading>PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES BILL.<br/>IN COMMITTEE.</heading>

<p>On clause 13,</p>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>had moved to omit the words &#x201C;so far as practicable&#x201D; in line 56, and in line 57, after &#x201C;gaol,&#x201D; to insert the word&#x2019;s &#x201C;except for the purposes of transit from the place of punishment to the road camp.&#x201D; He said he noticed that the Minister of Justice, in the Estimates, notwithstanding that in this Bill he had got to make provision for increased accommodation, had diminished the amount that he had got to ask. Altogether there was a reduction of &#x00A3;42,000.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#becker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. BECKER</person> (Ladismith)</from>

<p>said the amendments which had been moved would be practically impossible in some country districts. Supposing a first offender was arrested, he would have to spend the first night in gaol, because there would probably be no other place to put him. If the Minister were to provide special accommodation in all the districts of the Colony there would be no end to the expenditure. He certainly did not think it was possible to accept the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>was understood to say he did not believe the amendment was practicable.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>moved: On page 10, line 2, after &#x201C;describe,&#x201D; to omit &#x201C;it&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;the locality where the road camp is stationed.&#x201D;</p>

<p>The amendments proposed by the Minister of Justice in lines 51 and 54 were agreed to.</p>

<p>The amendments proposed by Sir H. H. Juta were negatived.</p>

<p>The amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice on page 10 was agreed to.</p>

<p>The clause, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 14,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>moved, after the word &#x201C;Minister&#x201D; in line 20, to insert &#x201C;and authorised by Law.&#x201D; Under the clause as it now read, he said, the gaolers were bound to receive anybody under a warrant signed by a Minister. He wished to qualify that by providing that the gaoler should only receive a prisoner under a warrant signed by the Minister when authorised by law.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said it was possible that a Minister might make a mistake, and the consequences of the amendment would be that they would make an unfortunate gaoler responsible.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that the amendment really took away a burden which the Minister sought to impose on the gaoler.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that under the clause, as it stood, the Minister was responsible.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that under section 95 the gaoler, as an officer, was responsible.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said: that if a gaoler were to do anything illegal under a warrant issued by the Minister, he would certainly be protected by Parliament. His point was that they should not saddle the gaoler with the responsibility of deciding whether a warrant was authorised by law.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>thought the amendment was reasonable. As it was, they give the Minister power to apprehend anybody, and did not fix the responsibility on him.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said the liberty of the subject was affected. In this clause, they proposed to take away the right of the individual. It was not a question of the gaoler&#x2019;s position.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said the clause did not give authority to any Magistrate or police officer to arrest any person.</p>

<p><span class="col_1255-1256" refersTo="page_0637"/>Such officer would still be responsible as under common law. The clause merely put the gaolers in the position of being able to harbour any arrested person.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>Said that, as far as he understood the Act of Union, they kept the Minister of Justice out of all matters of this sort. Under this Bill the Minister of Justice could issue a Warrant placing any man temporarily in gaol.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>That is a new point.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort):</from>

<p>The whole object of the Act of Union was that the Minister of Justice should be entirely dissociated from any criminal work whatsoever.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>It is purely an executive matter.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#phillips">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. PHILLIPS</person> (Yeoville)</from>

<p>said he could not for a moment understand why the Minister of Justice resisted the introduction of the simple words which would compel him to act under the law. As the words stood at present, a gaoler must accept a man on the order of the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he hoped the hon. member would understand the position. They had nothing to deter the Minister from issuing a warrant to detain a man They added nothing to his responsibility. &#x2018;If he issued a Warrant he Would be liable not merely as a Minister, but according to law. A provision of this sort might be very important, say, in a time of mutiny. (&#x201C; Ah!&#x201D;) The whole safety of the State might depend upon that act of the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that the Minister of Justice had uttered sentiments which were about the last sentiments that he would have thought would have come from his mouth. Did he know that there was no tyranny that had been performed by Governments but had been justified by sentiments like that? To give Ministers the opportunity of issuing warrants and clapping people in gaol&#x2014;what a convenient thing it would be to have his friends opposite, on the eve of an election, clapped in gaol! (Laughter.). Joking apart, they paid too little regard to the liberty of the subject and laws bearing upon the liberty of the subject in this country. In every other constitution he thought, the better part of it had been taken up by laws to safeguard the liberty of the subject, and here in this Country, where during the last few years they had had some of the most lamentable instances of tyranny and oppression, they were going to strengthen the hands of the people whom a political party may have put in power for a few moments. He thought they were indebted to the hon. member for the Harbour Division for having brought to the notice of the House a clause: like this Their notice having been drawn to it, do let them assert the rights of freedom in this matter, and that no man should be put in prison except by the proper law, and not at the will of a Minister, however powerful he might befor the time being. The more powerful he was the more dangerous &#x2019;he would be. Let them think of the things that had been done in this country alone, of the iniquities that had been done by Ministerial authority.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#neser">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. NESER</person> (Potchefstroom)</from>

<p>said that he agreed with a great deal that had fallen from the right hon. gentleman who had just spoken, but he did not think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for the Harbour Division would have the effect that they were seeking.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vosloo">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VOSLOO</person> (Somerset)</from>

<p>said he did not wish to express an opinion as to whether the power the Minister claimed was just pr not, but he did wish to point out that it was in accordance with the present law of the Cape. He was rather surprised to hear the hon. members for Victoria West and Cape Town, Harbour (Mr. Merriman and Sir Henry Juta), because under the old Cape system the present provision existed, and neither of them, as a Minister of the Crown or as a member of Parliament, had made any attempt to alter it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>Which law&#x2014;where is it?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vosloo">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VOSLOO</person> (Somerset)</from>

<p>said that a Minister could issue a fiat to arrest a man on the affidavit of any private person.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>Under martial law?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vosloo">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VOSLOO</person> (Somerset):</from>

<p>Not at all. Under the ordinary law.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#phillips">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. PHILLIPS</person> (Yeoville)</from>

<p>said that a Minister should not have power to send anybody to gaol unless he had due authority under the law. He took it, that on that point the whole House agreed. As regarded the remarks of the hon. member for Somerset (Mr. Vosloo), all he could say was that if such terrific things as he had described had taken place in the Cape, the time had arrived to put a stop to them. He was quite sure that the sense of the House would be in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cape Town, Harbour (Sir Henry Juta).</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West.)</from>

<p>said the hon. member for Somerset (Mr. Vosloo), who had spoken so learnedly, was Confusing the offices of the Minister of Justice and the Attorney-General. One of the best boons the Union had given was the distinction between the two. With regard to the accusation which had been made against himself and the hon. member for Cape Town, Harbour (Sir Henry Juta), that they had been Ministers of the Crown and had allowed the law to which the hon. member for Somerset (Mr. Vosloo) <span class="col_1257-1258" refersTo="page_0638"/>had referred to, all he could say was that the hon. member could not mention the law, and if there was such a law, well, there were a number of musty old laws which only required to (be brought to the notice of the House to be repealed. Why, only 100 years ago a man, charged with murder, claimed the right of ordeal by battle, and a law had to be repealed to defeat his object.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>said the Minister of Justice had stated that he could only act within the law. Why, he asked, therefore, did he object to the insertion of the amendment?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watt">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. WATT</person> (Dundee)</from>

<p>moved an amendment: That the following be a new paragraph, viz.: &#x201C;(g) When authorised there to by any law, or any order, rule or regulation having the force of law.&#x201D; He said that under his amendment the right which the Minister seemed to value would be preserved to him. As the Jaw stood at present it was far too autocratic a power to leave in the hands of a Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#clayton">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. F. CLAYTON</person> (Zululand)</from>

<p>asked if the Minister had any precedent in the matter?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he would move an amendment which, he hoped would commend itself to the House. He did not want, and did not appreciate, the authority to issue warrants. His amendment was to delete the word &#x201C;Minister&#x201D; and to insert the words, &#x201C;in any case upon the warrant granted under the hand of any person authorised thereby under the law. &#x2026;&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>and Mr. T. WATT (Dundee) withdrew: their amendments in favour of the Minister&#x2019;s amendment, which was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>moved in line 6 to omit &#x201C;and&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;or&#x201D;; and in line-27, after &#x201C;hospital&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;(other than a hospital used exclusively as an infectious diseases hospital).&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>pointed out several discrepancies in the translation of the Bill. The translation was so had that the same set of terms was rendered in different ways.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#macneillie">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. C. MacNEILLIE</person> (Boksburg)</from>

<p>said in the Transvaal it was possible to send a patient to a lunatic asylum for seven days, for the purpose of observation. It was unfair to the nursing staff of general hospitals to send lunatic patients to them. He was assured; that there were numerous cases of persons being despatched to asylums who should not have been sent there, as their mental trouble frequently lasted only two or three days, and ten they left the asylums with a stigma renting upon them. It would be better for such <b>j</b> patients to be treated in a special ward in a general hospital.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watkins">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. H. WATKINS</person> (Barkly)</from>

<p>said a difficulty would arise in such towns as Kimberley, where a mental patient would be refused admission by both hospital and gaol.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that a prison was not the proper place for a poor man or woman mentally deranged. In many cases hospital authorities refused to come to Government&#x2019;s assistance in this matter, with the result that Government was constantly being embarrassed with such cases. Where there was accommodation, a hospital was the place for these people. (Hear, hear.) If the present hospital staff was not large enough to cope with such cases, the hospitals should get additional assistance. They asked the hospital authorities to supply this accommodation for lunatics, but he was afraid the hospital authorities did not like this class of patient, and did not like to take the trouble with him, and consequently they sent him to the gaol. This was a very wrong procedure.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town. Gardens)</from>

<p>said the Minister of Justice did not evidently understand the position of a great number of hospitals in this country. They were entirely unsuitable for the treatment of lunatics. They had no provision for male nurses, and so it was impossible for them to deal with male lunatics. Even to suggest that they should deal with this class of patient was almost in the nature of a scandal. It seemed to him that the poor lunatic would fall between two stools. The hospitals, as they were constituted to-day, were entirely unsuitable for lunatics.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watkins">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. H. WATKINS</person> (Barkly)</from>

<p>said he entirely sympathised with the Minister of Justice in his endeavour to keep lunatics out of gaol, but he had not provided for their accommodation. This procedure would not bring pressure to bear upon the hospitals to make them take in lunatics. He did not believe that any district surgeon or magistrate would send a man to gaol if there was accommodation for him. The Minister of Justice was, in a sense, the father of all the lunatics in the country&#x2014; (laughter)&#x2014;and he ought to see that proper accommodation was provided for them. It seemed easy to say that they would only have to detain a man 48 hours or so in a hospital, but; in reality, it meant perhaps 48 days. A magistrate would not sign an order for a lunatic to go away until he was informed if they had accommodation for him. The real position was that this clause would not help one little bit; it would not put pressure upon the right people.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Capes. Town Central)</from>

<p>said he sympathised with the poor lunatic, and it seemed a pity that she should be sent to goal but he would point out that the pressure would some <span class="col_1259-1260" refersTo="page_0639"/>from the hospital authorities, who would instruct their members to move in the matter. He hoped the Minister would stand by the clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#macaulay">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. MACAULAY</person> (Denver)</from>

<p>reminded the hon. member for Boksburg (Dr. Mac-Neillie), as one who had charge of a lunatic asylum, that the best thing to do, under the circumstances, was to leave well alone.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>said if there was one thing that should not be done it was to open the wards of a hospital to patients suffering from mental afflictions to the discomfort and perhaps danger of the other patients. It was unfortunate that mental sufferers should have to be confined temporarily in gaol, but whatever the solution might be for the accommodation of lunatics, it should not be in finding them accommodation in the hospitals under present conditions.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#macaulay">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. MACAULAY</person> (Denver)</from>

<p>said that the hon. member (Mr. Maydon) was labouring under a delusion in imagining that anyone suffering mentally was put in wards with other patients. Sufferers from acute delirium were always placed apart.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said he greatly sympathised with the desire to keep lunatics out of gaol. He was personally acquainted with cases up-country, where people from respectable families, suffering from mental derangement, had been forced into gaol to herd with criminals. If they had hospitals which had the necessary accommodation, surely it was reasonable to expect that anyone afflicted mentally should have temporary accommodation in an hospital, instead of shoving him into gaol. He had known cases in which most respectable persons suffering temporarily from mental diseases had been put in gaol and herded with some of the most degraded of the population. He agreed that if this were passed, it would have the effect of bringing pressure to bear on the responsible Minister, and that it would then become the duty of the Government to make adequate provision for special wards for people of that description. He would rather see hospitals put to temporary inconvenience than see respectable people, who had committed no fault, sent to herd with criminals in a common gaol.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#long">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">B. K. LONG</person> (Liesbeek)</from>

<p>thought that if the proposal were agreed to they would only be sacrificing the interests of the lunatic, for while they were making provision for his reception the lunatic would be wandering about between the hospital and the gaol. Surely, the best way would be to make it a condition of the grants to hospitals that they should make such provision.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#macneillie">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. C. MacNEILLIE</person> (Boksburg)</from>

<p>said he differed from the hon. member for Fort Beaufort. Medical men, he thought, might be trusted only to send cases to hospitals or asylums, when it was absolutely essential. In his experience, lunatics were not herded with criminals in gaols: the patients were isolated in such cases He would agree to drop his amendment if the Minister would agree to add the words: &#x201C;where provision is made for the reception of such cases.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town Central)</from>

<p>hoped the amendment would not be pressed. It would simply mean that the hospitals would say: &#x201C;We have no accommodation&#x201D;; and then the un fortunate lunatic would have to go to gaol. The only way to remedy the existing state of affairs was by bringing the pressure of public opinion to bear on the Government&#x2014;first on the Treasurer, who had the money, and then on the Minister of the Interior.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#becker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. BECKER</person> (Ladismith)</from>

<p>favoured provision being made whereby a lunatic should not be kept in gaol for more than three weeks or a month. Then the Government would be compelled to provide accommodation in the asylums. He knew of cases in which lunatics had been kept in gaol for three months on the ground that there was no accommodation in the asylums.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fitzpatrick">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. P. FITZPATRICK</person> (Pretoria East)</from>

<p>said there would be a great difficulty in many of the smaller hospitals in providing accommodation for lunatics under existing circumstances. If the policy of having provision for lunatics in hospitals were adopted, provision should be made not only in the matter of room, but for nursing as well. It would not be right to tax the present nursing staffs with this further work.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said his point was that the hospitals were really the places where these lunatics should be, and if they had not proper accommodation in the hospitals, then they must provide it elsewhere. He knew that numbers of lunatics were kept constantly in gaol.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chaplin">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. D. P. CHAPLIN</person> (Germiston)</from>

<p>said that they were faced with a difficulty in connection with this clause, and now it was prepared to meet it by putting a spoke in the wheel. The thing should be settled between the two departments, or this clause was going to be a dead letter, or lead to ludicrous consequences. The gad was most inadequate, and in many cases the most improper place for cases of this kind.</p>

<p>Dr. MacNeillie&#x2019;s amendment was negatived, whereupon he called for a division, but withdrew his request shortly afterwards.</p>

<p>The clause, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p><span class="col_1261-1262" refersTo="page_0640"/>On clause 15,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watkins">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. H. WATKINS</person> (Barkly)</from>

<p>said that in the Bill he found no provision made for the amount of bard labour which a person did being regulated by the medical officer. He moved the insertion of the words: &#x201C;and approved of by the medical officer.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>thought that sufficient provision had already been made in the clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>supported the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that the superintendent might put the person detained to easy work. What the hon. member (Dr. Watkins) wanted was to give the medical officer the right to interfere.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that under section 85 regulations were to be framed in regard to medical officers. The regulations which were to be framed were in force, and to-day a medical officer could say, and did say, from day to day with regard to any prisoner who was ill: &#x201C;Don&#x2019;t let him do this or that, or treat him in such-and-such a way.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that this clause did not refer to hard labour prisoners, but to people who were accused of a crime, and had not yet been tried. He thought his hon. friend (Dr. Watkins) would withdraw his amendment if the Minister would give the House the assurance that in clause 86 he would insert power to make regulations to give a medical officer every right which the Minister said the medical officer now had. Under clause 86 at present there was no such power.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>referred to a difference in the English and Dutch translations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said that it was the duty of the Government to see that so far as possible the Dutch and English wording of Bills should be exactly the same. He could imagine that if that were not done serious confusion would ensue.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#theron">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. S. THERON</person> (Hoopstad)</from>

<p>drew attention to the defective translation of the Bill.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watkins">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. H. WATKINS</person> (Barkly)</from>

<p>said he was quite willing to withdraw his amendment, on the assurance of the Minister that the matter would be dealt with in the regulations. It was hopeless to expect amendments to be carried when every suggestion that was made was taken as a party attack. He could not see why things should be put into regulations which should be part of the (Bill. Here was a clear and definite thing, which could be dealt with perfectly easily in the Bill.</p>

<p>The clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 16, employment in gaols of civil debtors and certain other classes of prisoners,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>said that in this clause it was provided that anyone detained in gaol should be called upon to do a certain amount of work. This also applied to civil debtors, witnesses, and men awaiting trial. He could understand a man awaiting trial at least doing such labour as would keep himself and his surroundings clean, but he did think it was going too far to make such a stipulation in the case of a man who was not accused of anything, but who was being detained as a witness, and whose liberty already had been taken away from him. The rule meant that the man would have to do all sorts of menial labour.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>suggested the deletion of the words &#x201C;and any premises adjoining.&#x201D; Under the clause, a detained witness could be forced by the gaoler to perform the lowest of all duties a man could be called upon to perform in this or any other country. It seemed to him (Mr. Currey) a dreadful thing that a gaoler should have this power over a white man. He would like to see that power removed with regard to civil debtors (hear, hear)&#x2014;and he hoped, before (Parliament broke up, the whole law with regard to civil debtors would be altered. It was a relic of barbarism to put a man in gaol because he could not pay his debts.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said, under the circumstances, he thought it was best, and would move, that the clause stand over.</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 19, maintenance of civil prisoners,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said he would like to know what time constituted the first day&#x2019;s imprisonment of a civil debtor. They must have some reasonable (hour on which a debtor should enter or leave the prison, and therefore he thought they should have some uniform time. He would suggest that the day be deemed at 10 o&#x2019;clock to 10 o&#x2019;clock, 24 hours afterwards. He would move also that the clause stand over, so that the (Minister could give the matter his consideration. The motion was agreed to.</p>

<p>Clause 20 was verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 23,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>thought that the word &#x201C;continuous&#x201D; relating to separate confinement must have been inserted in error. As the clause stood, a prisoner could be separated from others for three years; then, after a month, he could be separated for a further period of three years. Thus, a convict undergoing a long sentence might spend practically the whole term in separate confinement. Out of a sentence of 15 years a man could do <span class="col_1263-1264" refersTo="page_0641"/>14 years and seven months in separate confinement. It would tend to drive a prisoner mad, and was altogether too severe.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>thought that one year was a sufficient period of segregation. The result of a man being segregated for even twelve months would be terrible enough. He moved, therefore, to make the first period one year instead of three years.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>did not think the clause was necessary. The matter could be dealt with under inter-departmental regulations. He would suggest that the clause should be omitted altogether.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>said he did not think the clause meant solitary confinement. He took it that it meant segregation. He moved to omit &#x201C;continuous&#x201D; from line 20.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>thought that a clause of this kind was necessary.: Long periods of segregation had not given rise to insanity. He went on to quote the periods of solitary confinement taken in other countries. One country, he said, had ten years&#x2019; solitary confinement.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>Russia, for instance. (A laugh.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>mentioned that Holland give five years&#x2019; solitary confinement, and that it was a very old system they had there.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville):</from>

<p>Yes, very old, and very bad. (A laugh.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>I have always heard a great deal to the contrary. Ho added that in view of the scale adopted in other countries, and from what the results were said to fee, he did not think three years were too much. He was prepared to strike out the word &#x201C;continuous.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>again pointed out instances of contradictions in the English and Butch texts.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>maintained that the meaning was the same, though a different phraseology might be used.</p>

<p>It was agreed that the word &#x201C;continuous&#x201D; should be omitted from the clause:</p>

<p>Mr. Schreiner&#x2019;s amendment was put and negatived, and clause 23 as amended was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 25, application of isolation and mechanical restraint,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that a little while ago the Minister said he perpetrated a joke, and that he (the speaker) did not see it. Might he ask whether this was another joke? Under clause 25, where it was necessary to secure a prisoner, they might use irons or some other mechanical restraint. But upon whom? Upon a prisoner who had escaped. (Laughter.) To say more would be superfluous. (More laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he saw the joke, and Would move the following amendment: In line 39, to omit &#x201C;escaped&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;been recaptured after escape,&#x201D; and to omit &#x201C;or&#x201D; at the end of the line; in line 4G to omit paragraph (c); in line 49 to insert the following new paragraph, to follow paragraph (2): &#x201C;(3) A superintendent, assistant superintendent, or gaoler may cause to fee isolated, and, if necessary, subjected, to mechanical restraint, any convict or prisoner if the isolation or restraint, is requested by the police authorities in the interests of justice, but the period of any such isolation or restraint shall not be longer than is necessary for the purpose required.&#x201D; In line 63 after &#x201C;death&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;or in course of transfer, or while temporarily outside the precincts of the convict prison or gaol&#x201D;; in the same line to omit &#x201C;there to&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;to solitary confinement by a Court of Law.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#long">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">B. K. LONG</person> (Liesbeek)</from>

<p>said the effect of the amendment was very similar to the provision in lines 41 to 44.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>said that in the English copy of the Bill occurred the phrase, &#x201C;alleged lunatic and feeble minded,&#x201D; while in the Dutch copy the phrase read, &#x201C;alleged lunatic or feeble minded. Which was correct?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>pointed out that, according to the amendment, an additional punishment was inflicted on Prisoners who escaped, because the Bill already made provision for dealing with escaped prisoners.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>This is only in special cases.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour):</from>

<p>Is this a, cumulative or a substituted punishment?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>It is not so much a punishment&#x2014;it is as little a punishment as the closing of a hospital door is.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#becker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. BECKER</person> (Ladismith)</from>

<p>said the intention of the clause 25 was simply to secure a man until such time as he could be brought before a Magistrate, because it was not always possible to bring him at once before a Magistrate.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">Mr. J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>moved a verbal amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he was prepared to insert the words &#x201C;and long&#x201D; after the word, &#x201C;often&#x201D; in line 36.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>said that this was too much power to place in the hands of police authorities. He moved therefore, to delete the words &#x201C;requested by police authorities&#x201D; for the purpose of <span class="col_1265-1266" refersTo="page_0642"/>inserting the words &#x201C;authorised by a Magistrate.&#x201D; He pointed out that in the definition clause the word &#x201C;magistrate&#x201D; was Very wide it included five sets of officials. That was surely wide enough.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he thought it was necessary to give the police authorities these powers. There were often instances in which the police could not get hold of a Magistrate.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#berry">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. BERRY</person> (Queen&#x2019;s Town)</from>

<p>moved to report progress and ask leave to sit again.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>Let us finish the section. (Hear, hear.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>complained about inefficient translation.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment.</p>

<p>The other amendments were agreed to,</p>

<p>The clause, as amended, was adopted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>then moved to report progress.</p>

<p>Progress was reported, and leave obtained to sit again to-morrow.</p>

</speech>

<adjournment>

<p>The House adjourned at <recordedTime time="1911-02-16T23:30:00">11.30 p.m.</recordedTime></p>

</adjournment>

<debateSection name="#opening">

<heading>FRIDAY, February 17.</heading>

<prayers>

<narrative>

Mr. SPEAKER took the chair and read prayers at <recordedTime time="1911-02-17T14:00:00">2 p.m.</recordedTime>

</narrative></prayers>

<debateSection name="#petitions">

<heading>PETITIONS.</heading>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort),</from>

<p>from L. A. Burnell, Railway Department, accountant.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#van_niekerk">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. A. VAN NIEKERK</person> (Boshof),</from>

<p>from voters of Boshof, for railway communication for the North-western districts of the Orange Free State (four petitions).</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#bosman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. J. BOSMAN</person> (Newcastle),</from>

<p>from the Charlestown Local Board, praying that further Asiatic immigration be stopped.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#theron">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. S. THERON</person> (Hoopstad),</from>

<p>from the Village Management Board and residents of Odendaalsrust, O.F.S., praying that further Asiatic immigration be stopped.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#pensions_grants_and_gratuities">

<heading>PENSIONS. GRANTS AND GRATUITIES.</heading>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#select_committee&#x2019;s_report">

<heading>SELECT COMMITTEE&#x2019;S REPORT.</heading>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>moved that the first report on the Pensions, Grants, and Gratuities Committee be now considered.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#krige">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. J. KRIGE</person> (Caledon)</from>

<p>seconded.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#hewat">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HEWAT</person> (Woodstock)</from>

<p>said before the House proceeded to consider the report, he would like the chairman to explain whether certain petitions from Civil Servants with regard to the privilege of paying back two years&#x2019; subscriptions for participation, in the benefits of the Pension Fund had been considered.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>said he recollected some cases to which the hon. member referred, and which had been considered some time past. All he would say was, they were all carefully inquired into, and the committee had by a majority come to the conclusion that no redress could be given. With regard to these particular cases, they were all examined individually. It was found that the petitioners had the opportunities mentioned, but they had not taken advantage of them and on that ground the committee held that they could not grant them the privilege. He would like this to be perfectly clear, the applicants had in most cases a double opportunity of contributing, but they had not availed themselves of the chance.</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to, and the recommendations were adopted.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#ostriches_and_angora_goats_bill">

<heading>OSTRICHES AND ANGORA GOATS BILL.</heading>

<speech by="#jameson">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. S. JAMESON</person> (Albany)</from>

<p>said he wished to ask the Prime Minister a question with regard to the Ostriches and Angora Goats&#x2019; Export Prohibition Bill. Many hon. members had been to him on the subject, and they were getting alarmed at the Bill gradually going lower and lower down on the paper. He had been informed that communications had been received by some hon. members that ostriches were actually being exported to German territory at the present moment. Therefore, those who were interested in the subject were distinctly anxious that this Bill should be brought forward as soon as possible.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>said that the Bill would come up in the ordinary course of business, but there were certain matters which the Government had to take into account, which rendered it impossible for the Bill to be brought up just now.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#public_accounts_committee_the_estimates_the_railway_estimates">

<heading>PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE.<br/>THE ESTIMATES.<br/>THE RAILWAY ESTIMATES.</heading>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>proposed, as an unopposed motion that votes 1 to 12, inclusive of the Estimates for the year ending March 51, 1912, be referred to the Public Accounts Committee for consideration. The House would remember that when he moved for the appointment of the Public Accounts Committee, he intimated that it was the intention of the Government to use it for the purpose of considering a certain section of the annual Estimates, the Government&#x2019;s intention being that the Estimates should be divided into three sections, and that one section should closely be examined each year by the committee. The section which it was proposed the committee Should examine this session included the votes for the Governor-General, the Senate, the House of Assembly, joint Parliamentary expenses, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, <span class="col_1267-1268" refersTo="page_0643"/>and the Minister of the Interior, Mines, and Defence. He did not know whether the Minister of Railways would follow the same course with regard to the Railway Estimates.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#louw">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">G. A. LOUW</person> (Colesberg)</from>

<p>seconded.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>hoped this would not be taken as a precedent. He thought these 12 votes would be as much as the Public Accounts Committee would be able to examine during the remainder of the session, but on future occasions he thought the whole of the Estimates should be referred to the Public Accounts Committee. He hoped the Minister of Railways would tell the House if the Railway Estimates would be referred to the committee.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>said he would tell his hon. friend when he (Mr. Sauer) laid his Estimates on the table, but he thought it would then be found that the Railway Estimates would be in such order that it would be a question whether it would be worth while referring them to the committee.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>asked when the Railway Estimates would be laid on the table?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>replied that they would probably be ready on Monday.</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#prisons_and_reformatories_bill_in_committee">

<heading>PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES BILL.<br/>IN COMMITTEE.</heading>

<p>On clause 27, penalty on convicts or prisoners, for escape or attempting to escape,</p>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>complained about incorrect translation, and said that this applied to several Bills.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>moved in line 16 to omit &#x201C;or by a visiting Magistrate,&#x201D; and in line 24 to omit &#x201C;and a visiting Magistrate.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he did not see why a Magistrate should be less inclined to do justice in gaol than when he sat in his own court. In the circumstances of the country he did not think it would be wise to accept the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>said that he hoped the Minister would not take these steps on their part to improve the Bill as irksome or objectionable. The Minister had not answered the one point of publicity. It was proposed in this clause to give the Magistrate additional power to inflict punishment up to two years&#x2019; imprisonment and 24 lashes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>said that in this clause they did not even provide that the Visiting Magistrate&#x2019;s sentence should be reviewed by a judge. A moment later, however, he stated that he was informed that in another clause review by a judge was provided for. He thought that in all oases, except of minor offences, trials should be conducted in the courts, with the representatives of the press present.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smuts">

<from>&#x2020; General <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. SMUTS</person> (Ermelo)</from>

<p>said that he thought that at present a Magistrate had power to impose a sentence of two years, or inflict lashes, in certain cases. He did not see any new principle in the clause under consideration; and if that clause had to be amended, other matters had to be altered as well. He thought that there should not be a tendency to make prison life too much of a heaven on earth&#x2014; (laughter)&#x2014;because he knew that there were natives for whom prison life had no terrors at all; quite the opposite, in fact; and when they came out, they spoke loudly of the easy time they had had, the good food, better than they got from their masters, and so on. They often did their level best to get back to that Land of Cockaigne!</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>said that if they took the Dutch version of the Bill, hon. members on that side need not trouble about sub-section 3, because it was there said that the Resident Magistrate or Visiting Magistrate should &#x201C;take cognisance.&#x201D; Read in English, the clause sounded serious; read in Dutch, it was perfectly preposterous. It all depended, therefore, on which version the Governor-General would sign.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#duncan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. DUNCAN</person> (Fordshurg)</from>

<p>said he hoped the Minister of Justice would accept the amendment. It was desirable that these cases should be tried in an open court, so that there may be publicity. He did not object to that jurisdiction being conferred upon the Magistrate, because a case like that could not be conveniently held over until it could be tried by the High Court; but he thought that the trial should be open.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_native_affairs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF NATIVE AFFAIRS</person></from>

<p>said that he sympathised entirely with the feelings expressed by hon. members opposite, and so did his hon. friend (General Hertzog), as regards an open trial of very serious cases. But he could not help feeling that rather too much had been made of these provisions in the Bill. The system of trying such offences within the prison was the one which prevailed all over the world. There was no publicity forbidden; and it was open for any member of the public to be present when the Visiting Magistrate held his inquiry at Tokai, for example. But he did not find people going to that court, which was quite open to them. (Laughter.) Theoretically, he was in favour of the views expressed by the other side, but in practice it was not convenient to the public at large that they should have such public trials of these offences, because it would mean battalions of convicts being sent to the Magistrate&#x2019;s Court. He could understand the objections of the hon. member <span class="col_1269-1270" refersTo="page_0644"/>(Mr. Quinn) if the prison officials were to conduct these inquiries, but that was not the ease, and the Magistrate conducted the inquiry. They had a man from outside, who was supposed to be a critic of prison discipline and the prison authorities.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said that the hon. member must see that they were not dealing with ordinary breaches of prison discipline, but with a special offence, which was treated specially.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that what was meant by publicity was the publicity given by the press, which could give a report of what was of public interest. He must take exception to what his hon. friend (Mr. Burton) had said. He had argued that the system in question prevailed all over the world; but because it prevailed all over the world, it was not necessarily good. They had had hideous revelations in past years of the prison system in England, and the dreadful things which had taken place in Van Diemen&#x2019;s Land. The great moral was: &#x201C;Don&#x2019;t get into gaol &#x201D;&#x2014;(laughter)&#x2014;but one could not help feeling some sort of sympathy with those poor creatures who got out of it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#crewe">

<from>Colonel <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. P. CREWE</person> (East London)</from>

<p>said that as regards Cape Town gaols, no one could get in without an order, and he was perfectly certain that in the desire of the superintendent to maintain order within the gaol it would be extremely difficult to get such an order, He thought that in a case where such severe penalties were provided as laid down in that section, they should adopt what the hon. member (Mr. Quinn) had proposed. It was right that trials for offences against prison discipline should be held within the gaol, for otherwise prisoners, for certain reasons, would take advantage of the trial being public, and the result would be an increase in the number of such contraventions of prison discipline.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he accepted the amendment, although he did not see that it would be advantageous.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>asked whether it was not too severe a penalty to impose 24 lashes for escaping or attempting to escape? Lashes were inflicted for certain brutal crimes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that the hon. member must not forget the class of offender they sometimes had to deal with. They might, in regard to prison escape, have to do with the very worst offenders, who had become so accustomed to prison life that it had no more terrors for them. They must be able, in certain very serious cases, to impose lashes, or otherwise hon. members would see what the consequences would be.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>said that there was no provision for the sentence to be confirmed by a judge. (An HON. MEMBER: &#x201C;Clause 57.&#x201D;) Clause 37 did not do that at all.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#crewe">

<from>Colonel <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. P. CREWE</person> (East London)</from>

<p>pointed out two years and 24 lashes were the maximum penalty, and there was no doubt that a maximum penalty was necessary in the case of very hardened criminals.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>wanted to know whether a man sentenced to five years&#x2019; imprisonment, who attempted to escape, was captured, tried, and sentenced to two years&#x2019; imprisonment and 24 lashes, would be be lashed at the end of his sentence, or when? (Laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said the lashes doubtless would be inflicted as soon as possible.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>pointed but a discrepancy between the English and Dutch versions of the Bill.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>said there was a worse instance in the clause as well as the next of the very slovenly way in which the two versions were drawn up. This was a responsibility that rested more upon the Ministerial side of the House than the other. It was extraordinary that hon. members would not see that there was exactness in the drafting of the Dutch and English versions. He would assure hon. members opposite that this was going to have a very serious effect upon the country. People might find that they had been looking at the wrong version all the time, and this would involve considerable legal expense. Surely it was the duty of the Minister to see that these Bills corresponded in the two languages as far as possible. It was not fair to the public to have these discrepancies.</p>

<p>An amendment to the Dutch version of the clauses, moved by Mr. C. L. Botha, was negatived.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that if hon. members wished to criticise, they ought at least to be well informed. The hon. member objected to the expression &#x201C;neemt kennis,&#x201D; but this was equivalent, in the jurisprudence of Holland, to saying that there should be jurisdiction.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>pointed out that they were legislating not for Holland but for South Africa, and in this country the words meaning &#x201C;takes cognisance of&#x201D; did not mean that there was special jurisdiction. Neither the Statutes of, nor the judgments delivered in, South Africa could be quoted in support of the Minister&#x2019;s peculiar terminology.</p>

<p>The clause as amended was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 28, rewards for apprehension of escaped prisoners,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#mentz">

<from><span class="col_1271-1272" refersTo="page_0645"/>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. MENTZ</person> (Zoutpansberg)</from>

<p>said the hon. member for Bloemfontein (Mr. Botha) bad pointed out defects in the Dutch Bill, but had overlooked discrepancies in the English Bill. The hon. member need not concern himself so much about the Dutch version, especially since he was such a strong advocate of the English tongue.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>said the hon. member for Zoutpansberg had suggested that he (Mr. Botha) was known to be a strong supporter of the English language as against the Dutch. That was the sort of remark he (Mr. Botha) could treat with the contempt it deserved. So long as the two Bills corresponded, he was content. A Dutch person might get held of the Dutch version of a Bill and consider that it was the one that was in force, but he (Mr. Botha) assumed that in most cases the Governor-General-would sign the English Bills, English being the only language His Excellency knew. Be (Mr. Botha) was trying to help the Dutch, but the hon. member for Zoutpansberg did not like him to do that.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#mentz">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. MENTZ</person> (Zoutpansberg)</from>

<p>moved to insert in line 32, after &#x201C;prisoner,&#x201D; the words &#x201C;or persons held under legal warrant.&#x201D;</p>

<p>The amendment was adopted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#duncan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. DUNCAN</person> (Fordsburg)</from>

<p>moved that the words, &#x201C;out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund,&#x201D; in line 33, be omitted.</p>

<p>The amendment was adopted.</p>

<p>The clause as amended was agreed to. On clause 29, powers of officers in reference to convicts or prisoners attempting to escape,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>moved to insert in the second line, between &#x201C;or&#x201D; &#x201C;and attack,&#x201D; the words &#x201C;threaten to attack,&#x2019;&#x2019; and after &#x201C;person&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;or in concert with others commit any act of violence.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>was surprised that an officer was empowered to fire upon a prisoner simply for attempting to escape.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he thought there was something in what the hon. member said. It was for the purpose of not waiting until a violent attack was made upon a man in gaol.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>said he thought that there should be an inquiry provided for under the third subsection.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>In every case there is an inquiry.</p>

<p>The clause as amended was agreed to. On clause 30, penalty for aiding escape,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#crewe">

<from>Colonel <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. P. CREWE</person> (East London)</from>

<p>said that they were going to create a new kind of crime in this clause. It was there laid down that a man may be dealt with for &#x201C;showing a desire to aid any convict or prisoner in escaping, or in breaking any regulation.&#x201D; He moved that the last five words be expunged.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town Castle)</from>

<p>said that they were proposing to deal with a purely mental crime. He would propose that all the words from &#x201C;showing a desire&#x201D; to &#x201C;regulation&#x201D; be deleted. They would never be able to obtain a conviction on this part of the clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that if the clause were what the hon. member who had just spoken said it was, he would accept the amendment. The clause should read as a whole, and not split up into portions.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#crewe">

<from>Colonel <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. P. CREWE</person> (East London)</from>

<p>said he did not think it was desirable to extend the jurisdiction of the Resident Magistrate&#x2019;s Court by putting little separate paragraphs into Bills</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle)</from>

<p>repeated that they were wanting to punish a man for a purely nebulous offence.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#grobler">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. W. GROBLER</person> (Rustenburg)</from>

<p>thought that from what the hon. member had said he had not read the clause. How often were prisoners not assisted to escape by means of signs? The guilty parties in such cases richly deserved punishment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#clayton">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. F. CLAYTON</person> (Zululand)</from>

<p>moved as an amendment, that the words &#x201C;encouraging or inciting&#x201D; be deleted; and the following be inserted: &#x201C;which encourages or incites&#x201D;; also that the &#x201C;or showing&#x201D; to taken out and &#x201C;which shows&#x201D; inserted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>considered that the clause was too vague. He hoped it would be deleted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he could not agree to the clause being taken out, as it was essential. If a man wrote a letter to a convict, saying: &#x201C;Kill your guard&#x2014;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central):</from>

<p>That is &#x201C;incitement.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>Or stated that he had a horse waiting&#x2014;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle):</from>

<p>That is &#x201C;encouragement,&#x201D; which is provided for already.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that, suppose such a letter encouraging a prisoner to escape did not reach the prisoner, but was intercepted by a guard, should not the sender of the letter be punished? He could not accept amendments simply because they arose in the minds of hon. members. He wanted good cause shown. (Hear, hear.) The Hill had been extremely well considered by the Commission, and he had carefully gone through it himself twice or thrice.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from><span class="col_1273-1274" refersTo="page_0646"/>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central):</from>

<p>Suppose I write to a friend in prison that I wish he were out. I should come under this clause of yours. (Laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>asked why the English version of the clause could not be divided into sub-sections as had been done with the Dutch version? If the English sub-sections had been drawn up to correspond with the Dutch, it would have simplified matters considerably. He agreed with the hon. member for Cape Town (Mr. Alexander) as to what he had said about &#x201C;intention.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he quite agreed with the objections to the discrepancies in, the Dutch and English versions. Ho disliked these involved sentences as much as anyone. As far as the duplicated version was concerned, it would only be referred to by a Judge if he was in any difficulty or to guide him in any ambiguity.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>thought it would be as well to leave out the words, &#x201C;or breaking any regulation&#x201D; from the clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>stated that the reason the clause was drafted in that way was because there must be no commas or stops. Hon. members might smile, but he would point out that many persons&#x2019; property had depended on a comma. The hon. member pointed out also that in the clause there was no offence/in encouraging a prisoner to break, the regulations, but the moment there was a desire to do so there was the liability to punishment. He proposed, therefore, to insert the words &#x201C;or break the regulation&#x201D; after the word &#x201C;escape,&#x201D; and in line 54 to insert the word &#x201C;knowingly.&#x201D; It would be unjust to punish a person who was unaware of the contents of a letter. He proposed also to leave out the words &#x201C;encouraging or inciting any prisoner,&#x201D; for the purpose of inserting the words &#x201C;for the purpose of inciting, aiding, or encouraging a prisoner to break the regulations.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle)</from>

<p>drew attention to clause 34, where it was also made punishable to break the regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he was beginning to feel very hopeless about the Bill. The lawyers were the biggest trespassers this afternoon. The hon. member for the Harbour (Sir H. Juta) came in after the clause had been discussed, and practically settled to the satisfaction of everybody but himself, and made new proposals. He (General Hertzog), however, did not blame the hon. member for Tembuland, as he was not a lawyer. The amendment would reduce the whole section to an absurdity.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>referred to a visit he paid to some Hottentots at Roeland-street Gaol, who were to be handed over to the German authorities. One of the Hottentots asked him for a bit of tobacco, and as the poor fellow was not long for this world, he (Mr. Struben) would have given it had it not been against the regulations, and for the presence of a warder. Had he done so, under that Bill he would have rendered himself liable to two years&#x2019; imprisonment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#becker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. BECKER</person> (Ladismith)</from>

<p>moved the insertion in line 51 of the words &#x201C;or police cell.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said the amendments he had proposed were not the result of a hasty consideration of the Bill that afternoon, but were the result of notes made by him after a careful perusal of (the Bill during the recess.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>Made in a hurry.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour):</from>

<p>I rather think the Bill was made in a hurry. (Opposition cheers.) Proceeding, he pointed out that the writer of a letter urging a prisoner to escape might have it conveyed to the prisoner by a person&#x2014;a little child say&#x2014; who was unaware of its contents. Under the Bill the writer would not be punished, but the bearer would be.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#meyler">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. M. MEYLER</person> (Weenen)</from>

<p>pointed out that there was a complete difference between the drafting of the English and Dutch versions of the Bill. The clause under discussion was printed with subsections in Dutch, but without sub-sections in English. If the Dutch copy were signed by the Governor-General, a person might be charged under a certain sub-section of the clause under discussion, but in the English version of the Bill there was no mention of sub-sections at all. The Minister said he would see that this sort of thing should not occur in the future, but why should mistakes be made now? He suggested that the Bill should stand over.</p>

<p>The amendment proposed by Sir Henry Juta to insert &#x201C;to break a regulation,&#x201D; in line 56, was agreed to.</p>

<p>The amendments proposed by Colonel Crewe and Mr. Clayton, and the amendment by Sir Henry Juta in line 54, were negatived.</p>

<p>Clause, as amended, put and agreed to.</p>

<p>Mr. Alexander&#x2019;s amendment to omit the words from &#x201C;showing&#x201D; to &#x201C;escape&#x201D; was withdrawn.</p>

<p>Clause 30, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 33, penalty of officers selling to convicts and prisoners, or being interested in supply of articles to them,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from><span class="col_1275-1276" refersTo="page_0647"/>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>drew attention to several discrepancies between the English and Dutch versions of the clause. In one case they had three different expressions used in the Dutch for the same thing. They were, he added, reducing their ideal of the dual language to a complete farce. The hon. member accordingly moved certain amendments in the Dutch version of the Bill. He also moved in line 31 to omit &#x201C;discounts&#x201D; and insert &#x201C;commission.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he had listened very carefully and patiently, but some hon. members did not seem to appreciate the time of the House, and seemed to obstruct.</p>

<p>The amendment in line 31 was negatived.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>declared, on the same amendment in the Dutch, that the &#x201C;Noes&#x201D; had it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein):</from>

<p>On this amendment I am going to claim a division.</p>

<p>The amendment was to the effect that in line 37(page 17) of the Dutch version, after &#x201C;gevangene,&#x201D; the word &#x201C;ongemachtigd&#x201D; be inserted.</p>

<p>The result of the division was as follows:</p>

</speech>

<p>Ayes&#x2014;31.</p>

<p>Alexander, Morris.</p>

<p>Baxter, William Duncan.</p>

<p>Berry, William Bisset.</p>

<p>Botha, Christian Lourens.</p>

<p>Brown, Daniel Maclaren.</p>

<p>Chaplin, Francis Drummond Percy.</p>

<p>Crewe, Charles Preston.</p>

<p>Duncan, Patrick.</p>
